title: NHL record-breaker Ovechkin says current season will be his last
description: NHL all-time scoring leader Alex Ovechkin said Monday that the current season will be his last in the North American ice hockey league.In a statement, Ovechkin said he and his family had decided over the summer that it was time to call time on his NHL career at the end of this season.
fullText:
NHL all-time scoring leader Alex Ovechkin said Monday that the current season will be his last in the North American ice hockey league.

The Russian superstar left wing is in his 22nd season with the Washington Capitals, the team he has represented ever since arriving in the United States in 2005.

Ovechkin, 41, shared the decision first with his teammates in the locker room in a video shared by the Capitals on Monday.

"This is going my last year... it's very important (for) guys to know first. And yeah, it's sad, but you know, it is what it is," said captain Ovechkin.

In a statement, Ovechkin said he and his family had decided over the summer that it was time to call time on his NHL career at the end of this season.

"I love this game so much, but I know in my heart it's the right decision," he said.

"It was important for me to make this announcement before our first home game, so I have the chance to thank all the people around the game, everyone who has been so important to me and my family and helped me through good times and tough losses."

Ovechkin captained the Capitals to their first Stanley Cup championship in 2018.

His 929 goals and 141 game-winning goals rank first in NHL history. Ovechkin has also recorded 759 assists.

He is closing in on Wayne Gretzky's combined tally of 1,016 regular season plus playoff goals, needing to score just 11 more to overtake the great Canadian.

Ovechkin sparked controversy this past off-season by appearing in a Russian political video backing President Vladimir Putin ahead of elections, but later told reporters he had no hesitation in making the video for the United Russia Party.

"They asked me to do that. I said yes. So, simple as that," Ovechkin said.

"I'm Russian. I support my country."

Ovechkin's appearance in the video drew harsh criticism from some, with US Representative Joe Wilson calling on the NHL to review Ovechkin's involvement in the clip.

"The thing about video, I'm Russian," Ovechkin said. "As soon as I'm done playing hockey, I'm probably going to stay there. I'm going to live there. My kids are going to live there. Family.

"I'm for peace and love and I hope everything is going to be OK. My home is Russia and DC is my second home."

title: Defendant in Terrion Arnold kidnapping-robbery case pleads guilty
description: Boakai Hilton, 24, pleaded guilty in case in which ex-Lion Terrion Arnold is accused of coordinating a kidnapping and robbery in Florida.
fullText:
A Florida man has pleaded guilty in the alleged robbery and kidnapping plot linked to former Detroit Lion Terrion Arnold.

Boakai Hilton was sentenced to 10 years in prison Monday, according to the Hillsborough County State Attorney's Office.

Hilton pleaded to three counts of kidnapping, three counts of robbery with a firearm, conspiracy to commit kidnapping and conspiracy to commit robbery with a firearm.

He was one of seven individuals, including Arnold, who were charged in connection with the alleged plot to lure three men into a Tampa apartment and assault them. Defendants Lyndell Hudson, Freddie Lee Hughes III, Christion Williams, Jasmine Randazzo and Arianna Del Valle also were charged. Del Valle and Randazzo have pleaded guilty related to the case.

Arnold, who was staying in Florida at the time of the alleged assaults, has denied involvement. A phone message left for Arnold's attorney, Harvey Steinberg, for comment on the case was not immediately returned.

Arnold, 23, is accused of "coordinating and directing" the armed robbery and kidnapping in retaliation for thefts at a rental home in Largo, Florida. He allegedly believed the victims had stolen more than $200,000 worth of property from the Airbnb where he was staying, but prosecutors say there is no evidence linking the victims to the theft.

Prosecutors say Arnold was not present when the attack occurred, but that his car was outside the apartment during the incident and he participated in a group chat about it. He was released on bond in July.

The Lions released Arnold hours after a pretrial detention hearing in late June.

He signed with the NFL team, the Seattle Seahawks, in August.

This article originally appeared on The Detroit News: Defendant in Terrion Arnold kidnapping-robbery case pleads guilty

title: Monday Night Football: Saints TE Noah Fant is inactive; Falcons LB Samson Ebukam will play
description: The Saints will not have tight end Noah Fant for Monday Night Football.
fullText:
The Saints will not have tight end Noah Fant for Monday Night Football.

Fant is among the team's inactives.

He was questionable to play with an abdominal injury.

Rookie Oscar Delp should see more snaps behind starter Juwan Johnson.

title: Who are the top high school football teams in Northern California?
description: These are the top high school football programs in Northern California through Week 8 of the 2026 season.
fullText:
High school football in Northern California is heavily slept on, but doesn't go completely unnoticed.

De La Salle High School (Concord) moved up in the USA TODAY Sports Super 25 national rankings after a monstrous shutout, 42-0, against Cathedral Catholic. The Spartans are the only NorCal prep team nationally ranked in the USAT Sports Super 25.

Other California high schools ranked in USA TODAY's top 25 list include Southern California's Santa Margarita (Rancho Santa Margarita), St. John Bosco (Bellflower), Sierra Canyon (Chatsworth) and Mater Dei (Santa Ana).

Folsom High School (Sacramento) wasn't ranked in the USA TODAY Sports Super 25 national rankings, but was listed among the best football teams in the USA TODAY Sports Super 15 West region football rankings.

Here's where Northern California high schools rank nationally according to USA TODAY:

The Spartans are ranked at No. 20 on the USA TODAY Sports Super 25. They moved up from being ranked No. 23 in the previous week, as they come off their dominating 42-0 performance against Cathedral Catholic (San Diego). De La Salle improved to 6-0, remaining undefeated on the season.

QB Jaxon Loftin and Damari Dean connected for a 63-yard touchdown on the fifth snap of the game, and that ended up being all the Spartans needed. Loftin accounted for three touchdowns, adding two more on the ground. He threw for 140 yards and added 30 rush yards.

De La Salle was led on the ground by Duece Jones-Drew, son of former NFL running back Maurice Jones-Drew and UCLA commit, with 76 yards and a touchdown. Judah Pape had 63 yards on five carries and a tud.

Their defense was led by CJ Petersen, Zion Cadet and Prayshawn Harang. Petersen led the team with nine tackles including two for loss. Harang had seven tackles and a sack. Cadet made six tackles, including a sack.

De La Salle is atop the East Bay Mountain League, but they aren't alone at the top. There are two other teams without a loss at this point in the 2026 season. Monte Vista High School (Danville) is also 6-0, and San Ramon Valley is 5-0.

The Spartans will visit Monte Vista as both teams put their undefeated records to the test.

Monte Vista is coming off a 42-7 victory against Livermore behind a 231-yard, three-touchdown performance from junior quarterback Jimmy Lagios. Elijah Wood had two interceptions.

They face each other on Friday, Oct. 9 at 7:15 p.m. PST.

Folsom High School was the No. 10-ranked football team in the USA TODAY Sports Super 15 West region rankings. The Bulldogs are coming off a 43-7 win versus Granite Bay High School (CA) of Placer County. Folsom crossed the 200-plus points scored and fewer than 100 points allowed mark this season in their win.

Senior quarterback Brody Rudnicki completed 20-of-29 passes for 335 yards and six touchdowns. He threw one pick in the game. Senior receiver Travis Beatty led with seven catches for 122 yards and a touchdown. Arhian Acuna had two touchdowns on five catches and 62 yards, while sophomore Jaden Angel saw the end zone the most. Angel had three tuds on four catches for 91 yards.

The Bulldogs pulled away in the second half, and as the second half of the season is underway, they'll look to continue pulling away from competition and secure its spot as a top team in California entering the postseason.

They have been the darlings of the Sierra Foothill League and continue to head toward that trajectory with their leading 6-0 record and 2-0 in league games. Behind them is Whitney High School (Rocklin) who have a 5-0 record and 1-0 in league play and Oak Ridge High School (El Dorado Hills) is also undefeated at 2-0 in league, but have an overall record of 4-1.

It's an undefeated showdown in their next game when the Bulldogs host Whitney on Friday, Oct. 9 at 7 p.m. PST.

title: ‘That’s the talk’: Oscar De La Hoya negotiating Vergil Ortiz vs Keith Thurman
description: Oscar De La Hoya breaks down plans for several of his key fighters.
fullText:
Golden Boy promoter Oscar De La Hoya spends some time talking to Fight Hub TV about Floyd Schofield's weekend fight against Lucas Bahdi, plans for Vergil Ortiz to fight Keith Thurman on the upcoming David Benavidez undercard, why he wasn't at the Ryan Garcia vs Conor Benn fight, and more. Here's some excerpts of what he had to say with the full video interview below.

"When you get a kid like Schofield and take him to that world title, you help him, you try to guide him to that world title, it's so rewarding, it's so gratifying. Oct. 10, I do have to do my homework when it comes to how many world champions we helped. It's a lot. Since the beginning, it's got to be in the hundreds. So, I'm proud of what we do."

"It might not even be at 135 pounds. 'Kid' is a big kid. Kid Austin is a big '35 pounder and he's only growing. I really do believe 147 is going to be where Kid is going to shine, like really develop to this beast. I believe that weight class will be the pinnacle of his career. So, yeah, looking forward to those fights there and we all know the welterweight division is very hot right now.

"I strongly believe Kid can become undisputed at 135, 140, but 147 will be his weight class."

"Yeah, that's the talk. That's the talk, to fight him on the Benavidez card, which would be awesome. Imgaine Benavidez and Vergil Ortiz. I mean please, you'll sell out any arena, easy. We're working out things with Keith Thurman. It's not the opponent yet because things are being worked out but we're hoping that we can get Vergil's career back on track."

"I wish it would've been the Boots fight but we can't keep our fighter idol for so long. I mean, Boots is going to fight who, Kelly? Josh Kelly, is it? Then Fundora is going to fight somebody else. So, we had to keep Vergil busy and not idle and so Keith Thurman is one guy that's always willing to fight the best, which is very cool…That is the plan but you never know what happens after that, so we'll see."

"Everything's cool…Ryan had a great victory, I'm very happy for him that he was able to knockout Conor Benn obviously the way I expected. Look, people were saying 'oh my gosh, this is a huge fight.' No. It turned out the way I actually envisioned it. Conor Benn is a great fighter, don't get me wrong. He's a good fighter in the UK but there's a difference when you come fight in the US. It's just a whole different level."

"Ryan and I talked. He wanted me to walk him out…I have so much information. I've been keeping quiet, don't get me wrong. I cannot wait for this ultimate clap back. So I don't want to spill the beans here but it's going to be powerful…But me and Ryan, we're cool.

"I wasn't going to show up [after being asked not to come] to be embarrassed. I mean, it was a Zuffa f-ckin' event…But I was not going to show up to be embarrassed and that's exactly what they were going to do to me. I was not going to do that so I made the wise decision to not go."

"I never thought in my wildest dreams that I would be Team Eddie. I'm Team Eddie. I never thought I would be Team Eddie. He is cooking Dana White, it is hilarious. I think he took a book out of my edits that I do with my videos, posting Dana White videos and making fun of him and this and that. But it's crazy how Dana has no clue what's going on.

"They're asking him about boxing, they're asking him about the UFC, it's like, he doesn't know what's happening…I think Eddie Hearn has done a number on him and I'm laughing all the way to the bank."

title: Padres dismiss Mason Miller pitch-tipping speculation, prepare to face Brewers with season on line
description: — Although the San Diego Padres have plenty of concerns in the face of playoff elimination, they don't believe Mason Miller tipping his pitches is one of them.Padres manager Craig Stammen dismissed the widespread online speculation after Game 2 of the NL Division Series that the Milwaukee Brewers could tell what was coming from San Diego's vaunted closer when they rallied for two runs and a 4-3 victory in the ninth inning.
fullText:
SAN DIEGO (AP) — Although the San Diego Padres have plenty of concerns in the face of playoff elimination, they don't believe Mason Miller tipping his pitches is one of them.

Padres manager Craig Stammen dismissed the widespread online speculation after Game 2 of the NL Division Series that the Milwaukee Brewers could tell what was coming from San Diego's vaunted closer when they rallied for two runs and a 4-3 victory in the ninth inning.

"We've got a crew of people that are dedicated to that every single day," Stammen said Monday at Petco Park. "That is their sole job. We're well aware of what's going on with our pitchers, well aware of what's going on with the Brewers pitchers and how they do things. It's part of our daily (regimen). The internet can go crazy and take things farther than they need to go. We feel good about our process within that situation."

But the Padres are still smarting from Miller's blown save, which put them in an 0-2 series hole.

The All-Star closer threw only 21 of his 40 pitches for strikes over his two innings. The disciplined Brewers repeatedly laid off his sliders and errant fastballs while stringing together three walks in the ninth, followed by Jackson Chourio's two-out, two-strike, two-run single that won the game.

While Stammen didn't flat-out confirm the Padres are sure Miller wasn't tipping pitches, the manager downplayed the importance of the whole discussion.

"We've got a lot of guys on top of it, and we're not really worried about it," he said.

Even while facing a possible quick end to their 91-win season, the Padres can take confidence from the fact they were one strike away from splitting the first two games with the majors' best regular-season team.

Heck, many fans believe they were one strike and one roof cable away from claiming two wins in Milwaukee.

Instead, the Padres are on the brink of winter as they welcome the Brewers to Petco, where San Diego was largely outstanding all season. Game 3 is Tuesday night.

"It's not an easy job," Padres slugger Manny Machado said. "It's a tough road. You've got to deal with a lot of adversity. Here we are once again with our backs against the wall. We've overcome it once, and we can do it again — and we're going to do it again."

Nick Pivetta takes the mound for the Padres in their must-win game, and the veteran right-hander is grateful to be in this situation after he missed nearly five months of the regular season with a right elbow injury. San Diego's opening-day starter didn't pitch in the majors between April 12 and Sept. 7 while working his way back.

Pivetta believes the Padres have a roster capable of pulling off a comeback that's been managed by only 10 of the 93 MLB teams to fall behind 0-2 in a best-of-five series.

"We have a bunch of professionals in this room, a lot of really great players who have played in amazing games, who have World Series rings, that you can rely on in these moments," said Pivetta, who pitched one-run ball into the fourth inning of their Wild Card Series-clinching win over the Cubs last week. "Just coming together as a group is what I look forward to, and seeing us succeed as a group is going to be very special."

Dustin May starts Game 3 for Milwaukee, and the Padres' veterans know him better than most starters thanks to his several years with the rival Los Angeles Dodgers.

San Diego has faced May in 16 previous appearances since 2019. May faced the Padres three previous times this season, even throwing a one-hitter against San Diego for the Cardinals in June.

"We've had some history with May, but we've got to stick to our strengths, stick to what we've been doing," Machado said. "Ultimately it's about getting that big hit in those big moments, and if we can, we'll be all right."

title: Ben Johnson shares update on Kyle Monangai's injury
description: Bears head coach Ben Johnson provided an update on Kyle Monangai's hand injury suffered during Sunday's win over the Jets.
fullText:
The Chicago Bears had a bit of a scare after Sunday's dominating 23-12 win over the New York Jets when it was revealed running back Kyle Monangai suffered a hand injury during his incredible performance. Fortunately, though, it seems the injury won't be a serious issue for the bruising back.

Speaking with reporters on Monday afternoon, head coach Ben Johnson said he believes Monangai is going to be fine as it relates to his thumb injury and is considered day-to-day. "We think he's going to be okay, so we'll see what it looks like as we go through the week here," Johnson said. "More of a day-to-day deal."

Monangai was a workhorse on Sunday, rushing 30 times for 146 yards and two touchdowns. He also caught a pass for four yards as well. After D'Andre Swift fumbled in the third quarter, Monangai took on the vast majority of carries until the final drive when Roschon Johnson took over. We'll see what his availability looks like in practice, but it sounds like good news for one of the most important players on offense heading into Week 5 against the Green Bay Packers.

title: Clemson CB Corian Gipson out for season with knee injury. Here are Tigers' options
description: Clemson has taken a hit in its secondary, as starting nickel Corian Gipson will miss the rest of the season with a knee injury
fullText:
Clemson football coach Dabo Swinney said Oct. 5 that starting nickel Corian Gipson will miss the rest of the season with a knee injury.

Swinney said the junior will need surgery on his meniscus and that he'll "probably be out for a few months."

"I really hate that for him, as he had just gotten back," Swinney said. "That's a big, big loss for us."

Gipson played through his injury in the Tigers' 41-13 defeat to Miami on Oct. 3, collecting five total tackles, a forced fumble and a pass breakup.

Gipson first sustained a knee injury sometime during Week 3 ahead of the North Carolina game on Sept. 19, and played on the Tar Heels' first drive before sitting out the rest of the game. Gipson didn't make the trip to play California in Week 4 as a result.

Swinney said he re-aggravated his knee injury against the Hurricanes. After another MRI, Clemson's doctors recommended that Gipson's meniscus needed surgery.

"He really needs to fix the meniscus, so that's a big loss for us for sure," Swinney said.

Gipson was in his third season with the Tigers and his first as a full-time starter. He had 17 tackles across four games played.

Clemson (3-2) has an open week before playing Charleston Southern (2-3) at home on Oct. 17 (noon, ACC Network).

Senior Misun Kelley has been listed as Gipson's backup at nickel and has three tackles this year. He's in his fourth season with Clemson and his second as a defensive back. At 5-foot-9, Kelley is smaller than Gipson (6-foot-1) and is also 10 pounds lighter at 185.

Swinney also said that cornerback Donovan Starr, who's played 18 of his 36 snaps in the slot, and safety Ronan Hanafin could play more nickel with Gipson out. Freshman Marcell Gipson Jr. could also see the field more.

"Marcell is finally back healthy," Swinney said. "He was a kid that was really making some big strides for us in camp, then got hurt, missed a lot of time. He's been kind of ramping up these past couple weeks."

Star cornerback Ashton Hampton also played more at nickel against Miami, with his 24 snaps there being 17 more than his previous high this season. However, that was likely so he could cover star Hurricanes slot receiver Malachi Toney more often. If Hampton does play more nickel now, Swinney said cornerback Branden Strozier could play more on the outside.

Swinney also gave an update on senior running back Jay Haynes, who hasn't played since suffering an ACL injury in the 2024 ACC Championship Game against SMU.

Haynes was listed as out on the injury report for the Miami game, but for personal reasons, as he attended a funeral over the weekend. Swinney said Haynes is "just now getting back healthy" after some setbacks.

"He's a really good player," Swinney said. "When he's been healthy, when he's been available, especially in practice, we get excited, and then all of a sudden he's had some setbacks, and so he just hasn't had a chance to do anything... This is coming at a good time, as far as getting him back where he's healthy and can practice, and then got a couple weeks to get ready."

Haynes rushed for 295 yards and three touchdowns on 43 carries in 2024.

title: Cardinals’ Paris Johnson Jr. Out for Season After Brutal Giants Loss
description: The Arizona Cardinals were on the wrong end of a brutal loss to the New York Giants on Sunday, falling 36-24 at MetLife Stadium. It was not the only blow...
fullText:
The Arizona Cardinals were on the wrong end of a brutal loss to the New York Giants on Sunday, falling 36-24 at MetLife Stadium. It was not the only blow Arizona sustained in those 60 minutes of ugly football.

Toward the end of that disappointing contest, left tackle Paris Johnson Jr. went down with an injury. He remained in the game for a few plays, but eventually exited ahead of the very last play of the game — a 4th & goal throw that was intercepted and returned for a touchdown to seal it for the Giants. He was replaced by rookie OL Jayden Williams.

On Monday, Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur delivered bad news. When asked of Johnson's status, followed by a question regarding Williams' performance in relief, LaFleur deferred to the latter query first. Then, he announced that Johnson would miss the remainder of 2026 with a torn biceps — a brutal blow to an Arizona offensive line unit that already lacks significant depth.

Losing Johnson is more than simply a blow to the field, though it does certainly lower the level of offensive line play by a significant margin. He has had some trouble with injury, missing eight combined games at the latter portions of 2024 and 2025. He played all 17 in 2023, his rookie year.

Johnson, who is in the penultimate year of his rookie deal and expected to play on his fifth-year option in 2027, has been seeking a new contract. A significant injury could affect that deal's timeline.

"I feel for him, obviously," said LaFleur. "It sucks for him, first and foremost. It sucks, obviously, for the Arizona Cardinals, our offense, this team. But, you know, NFL football, here we are in October. The show goes on."

LaFleur said he did not know when Johnson would be undergoing surgery to repair his biceps, but said it is likely to happen "soon."

Arizona's head coach also spoke highly of Williams, who is projected to start going forward in Johnson's absence.

"I'm really, really impressed with Jayden," LaFleur said. "He's wise beyond his years. He obviously played big-time college football, so we've got a lot of confidence in him. Obviously, he's been doing some stuff in the 13-personnel game. When we go the two tight ends plus him, and he's not limited to just the run game, he can actually do some stuff."

Arizona also sustained an injury to their interior, as right guard Isaiah Adams left on a cart with an ankle injury. His exact status is not clear, but LaFleur said he is "most likely" out this coming week against the Detroit Lions at home.

And so, the Cardinals' projected starting offensive line looks like this, barring a late addition or elevation:

To put the blame of a rough offensive performance on the offensive line is not entirely honest, though that did play a factor in Sunday's loss. Jacoby Brissett was under a significant amount of pressure and delivered a poor game. He completed just 21 of 35 passes for 166, two touchdowns and three interceptions, including the game-ender. He was sacked twice and hit seven times by the Giants defense.

Arizona did run the ball relatively well with 123 yards on the ground, but managed only 270 total yards of offense. After two strong touchdown drives to open the game, the Cardinals had difficulty moving the ball without turning it over. Their defense allowed 319 yards of offense, squandering three turnovers by allowing New York backup QB Jameis Winston to find the end zone three times.

Despite that, there is no quarterback change on the horizon, LaFleur said. He added Arizona is not going to make large-scale changes to their process.

"We got to be better. And it starts with me in terms of the schematics, giving them a better advantage. Give them, like I said, better clarity," said LaFleur.

"We were 12 feet away. And I think if we could have got that ball in there, like I know we can, we're probably not even having a lot of these questions that I'm having to answer, which I respect all the questions. With that being said, it's not going to change our process."

The Cardinals will have to move forward offensively without a cornerstone piece in Johnson. Any improvements or changes will have to come with a more limited personnel group than they had going into Sunday's game.

Welcome to the NFL, where the Cardinals have continuously struggled to keep pace.

title: Karl-Anthony Towns, Knicks face stalemate on contract extension. Where do they go from here?
description: One of the huge questions facing the defending-champion New York Knicks is the future of star Karl-Anthony Towns. He doesn't sound so optimistic.
fullText:
It seems, in the case of Karl-Anthony Towns and the New York Knicks, that someone's going to have to blink first.

What's abundantly clear, however, is that there's a lot of work to do for the franchise to keep its star locked up in the long term, and the prospect that he may be playing his final months as a Knick are suddenly a real possibility.

Towns, the 30-year-old All-Star center who helped propel the Knicks to their first championship in 53 years, is eligible for a four-year extension. He had hoped to ink it before the start of the season. Yet, Towns expressed unfiltered pessimism Monday, Oct. 5 to reporters in Philadelphia, indicating just how far apart the two sides are.

"It don't look good," Towns told reporters when asked if he thought both sides could agree to a deal before the regular season opener October 20 against the Philadelphia 76ers.

KNICKS: After summer of adoration, New York gets back to business of title defense

Towns was even more candid later when asked if he thought he deserved a new deal.

"No (expletive), Sherlock," he said. "I just won a championship. You'd think it would be pretty easy, unless you guys think I have something else to prove."

Towns was instrumental in New York's historic postseason run. Aside from NBA Finals Most Valuable Player Jalen Brunson, Towns was easily the second-most important player on the Knicks, and it all started after New York lost two consecutive games in the first round against the Atlanta Hawks, to fall into a 1-2 series hole.

Knicks coach Mike Brown then tweaked the offense to run through Towns, instead of Brunson; Towns took on increased ball-handling and play-making duties, allowing Brunson to play off-ball and tactically choose his spots. The move unlocked a new dimension for New York's offense, whose +283 point differential smashed an all-time record.

But, to illustrate that point further, the Knicks were particularly dominant when Towns was on the floor. In his 578 postseason minutes, New York outscored opponents by 258 points, giving Towns the best individual plus-minus in a single postseason in the play-by-play era.

But, Knicks owner James Dolan has stressed multiple times that the Knicks will avoid triggering the punitive second apron, which limits financial flexibility. It also gives Knicks president Leon Rose a hard line on how much they can offer their stars. In a parallel situation, this also complicates the negotiations with forward Josh Hart.

KNICKS SEASON PREVIEW: Lineup, roster, prediction and biggest question mark

According to ESPN, the most recent Knicks offer to Towns was worth $200 million, which is well short – more than $75 million short – of what he's eligible to earn.

Now, none of this precludes the Knicks and Towns from eventually getting a deal done. In the NBA, like in all major sports leagues constrained by a salary cap, things get said in public that can sway perception. This is how high-profile negotiations sometimes work.

Towns and his representatives are trying to extract as much value as they can within New York's financial landscape. Dolan and the Knicks are trying to get their stars to play on team-friendly deals. At some point, for this partnership to continue, compromise is mandatory.

"Simply put: I want to do something that can keep this team together and work with the Knicks and also values me," he said. "None of those things have come close to happening."

This isn't exactly what a team looking to defend its title wants to be dealing with, but this is simply the system in place with the second apron to contend with.

The immediate concern for the Knicks, at least in the short term, is whether this will affect the team's play.

Towns has plenty of experience handling adversity; while the Knicks were slogging through their schedule in the first half of last season, his name frequently popped up in trade rumors. Towns eventually responded with that postseason run – the best basketball of his career.

Whispers of trade talks are one thing, but if a player feels undervalued, it's an entirely different issue to navigate. And the interesting thing is that those trade talks could get even louder.

Towns has a $61 million player option next season. While that is a lot of money, he may feel that he could earn even more on the open market. The Knicks, understandably, would not want to let a player like Towns, the premier stretch five in the NBA, hit the open market without getting anything in return. And a player like Towns – as we saw with the blockbuster that sent Giannis Antetokounmpo to the Miami Heat – would net a ton of assets.

So where does all of that leave us?

Right now, it's a game of chicken. And while Knicks fans shouldn't necessarily be concerned as of right now, these next few weeks and months will be pretty telling. Because the Feb. 11, 2027 trading deadline isn't all that far away.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Karl-Anthony Towns, Knicks face stalemate on contract extension. Where do they go from here?

title: Cardinals try to stave off frustration after 3-game losing streak
description: (AP) — The Arizona Cardinals were just 4 yards away from a galvanizing road win on Sunday.Eleven seconds later, they had lost 36-24 to the New York Giants in a dizzying flip after Jacoby Brissett's potential touchdown pass was intercepted by Deonte Banks and returned 98 yards for a touchdown as time expired.
fullText:
GLENDALE, Ariz. (AP) — The Arizona Cardinals were just 4 yards away from a galvanizing road win on Sunday.

Eleven seconds later, they had lost 36-24 to the New York Giants in a dizzying flip after Jacoby Brissett's potential touchdown pass was intercepted by Deonte Banks and returned 98 yards for a touchdown as time expired.

The whiplash was a microcosm for a frustrating stretch for these Cardinals (1-3), who look like a solid NFL team for much of their games, only to come up short at crucial moments.

There's plenty of football left to play this season, but the team's current three-game losing streak has brought a here-we-go-again feeling to the desert.

The Cardinals have a 20-52 record since 2022 and have been to the playoffs just once over the past decade.

First-year coach Mike LaFleur said Monday he's fighting to make sure his team isn't feeling sorry for itself.

"My message to them — amongst a lot of things — was we can't let the Giants beat us twice," LaFleur said. "We've got to move forward. So whatever you have to do once we get out of (meetings), which are ending right now, clear you head, get your mind right, get your body right, because when we get in here Wednesday it's full throttle for 1-0."

There are stretches where the Cardinals' offense looks great. Arizona took a 14-3 lead in the first quarter after two efficient drives that went 58 and 74 yards for touchdowns. Marvin Harrison Jr. scored the first TD on a 12-yard touchdown catch while Tyler Allgeier had the second on a 22-yard run.

The trick is sustaining that success for long stretches. Brissett blamed himself for throwing two interceptions in the second quarter that stalled momentum.

"I think we just kind of got in our own way again," Brissett said.

The Cardinals' offensive line is going to need an overhaul this week after the news that starting left tackle Paris Johnson Jr. is out for the season with a torn left biceps. LaFleur also said starting right guard Isaiah Adams (ankle) is probably out this week after getting hurt vs. the Giants.

Rookie Jayden Williams could be the starting left tackle on Sunday. The 6-foot-4, 307-pound Williams was a seventh-round pick out of Mississippi. Jon Gaines is the likely candidate to start at right guard if Adams can't play.

Edge rusher Josh Sweat had his best game of the season with four tackles, including two for a loss, two quarterback hits and a sack. Sweat is in the second year of a $76.4 million, four-year deal. Walter Nolen, Darius Robinson and Zaven Collins also had one sack each, giving hope that the young defensive line is making solid gains.

Brissett threw a career-high three interceptions against the Giants, including the 98-yard pick-6 that ended the game. The 33-year-old looks the part of an NFL quarterback and consistently piles up big numbers with the Cardinals, but he's struggled in the one stat that truly matters — wins.

Brissett has a 2-14 record with the Cardinals over the past two seasons and is 21-48 during his career as a starter.

"It's no magic words, but to turn the page," Brissett said. "It's let's get back to work, let's obviously correct it from the film and then, yeah, just get back to work. That's the only thing you can do."

LaFleur said Johnson (biceps) would have surgery soon so he can begin the recovery process. Safety Andrew Wingard (knee) left the Giants' game but LaFleur said the team got relatively good news on that injury and he would have an update on the veteran's availability later this week.

67 — The total number of points the Cardinals' defense has given up against two backup quarterbacks this season — Seattle's Drew Lock and New York's Jameis Winston.

The Cardinals host the Detroit Lions on Sunday.

See AP's full NFL coverage here

title: Former Houston Texans running back Joe Mixon, healthy again, signs with Seattle Seahawks
description: The Houston Texans running game hasn't been the same since Joe Mixon got hurt, and now their former running back is signing with the Seattle Seahawks.
fullText:
Joe Mixon, who hasn't played in an NFL game since January 2025, signed with the Seattle Seahawks on Monday, according to multiple reports.

Mixon, who rushed for 1,016 yards in his lone season with the Houston Texans in 2024, missed the entire 2025 season with a foot issue that Texans general manager Nick Caserio called a "medical condition." The running back wasn't around much of last season, leading to wide speculation about the injury, but Caserio said in January, "He didn't do anything off the field. It wasn't like he was riding a snowmobile or anything like that. I would say it was more a medical condition or situation that just - it didn't really improve as much as everyone would have hoped."

The Texans, who had signed Mixon to a three-year $27 million contract before the 2024 season, released him in March.

The defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks (3-1) are in need of a running back after placing rookie Jadarian Price on injured reserve Saturday.

Fox Sports' Jay Glazer reported Sunday that Mixon would visit the Seahawks and the running back posted a photo of the Seahawks stadium on Instagram on Monday evening.

The 30-year-old Mixon had posted back-to-back 1,000-yard seasons with the Bengals and Texans before sitting out 2025.

Without Mixon, the Texans have had trouble establishing a run game. Woody Marks led Houston with 703 yards on the ground last season. The Texans went out and signed David Montgomery in free agency, but so far, the former Detroit Lions running back has rushed for just 127 yards in four games. Marks has 87 yards on 28 carries so far this season.

There's more to Houston with the Chronicle. 

This article originally published at Former Houston Texans running back Joe Mixon, healthy again, signs with Seattle Seahawks.

title: ChatGPT is adding real cartoonists' signatures to fake New Yorker cartoons
description: OpenAI's chatbot isn't just imitating the magazine's style. It's also falsely attributing AI-generated images to real artists.
fullText:
At the pearly gates, Dolly Parton, in a sparkling gown, stands arm in arm with Tim Curry, dressed as Dr. Frank-N-Furter. “I knew I chose the right plus one,” Parton says to God, who is standing at heaven’s reception desk.

That’s the premise of a cartoon that went viral on Twitter in the days after the legendary entertainers’ deaths in late August. One tweet of the cartoon received 25,000 likes, while other versions of the image circulated on Facebook, Instagram, and Bluesky.

In the bottom right corner of the cartoon is the pen name “BLOPER,” the signature of New Yorker cartoonist Brendan Loper. But Loper didn’t draw the cartoon, or sign it. It was generated by ChatGPT and first posted to Facebook by a Dolly Parton fan. In the comments section of her post, she wrote she had simply asked ChatGPT to make “a New Yorker-style cartoon.”

“I had people writing to me about this cartoon, asking if it was mine,” Loper told me. First came a text from his twin brother, whose friend had seen the AI-generated image. Emails and DMs on social media from strangers followed. “It was very surreal,” he said.

This wasn’t the first time ChatGPT had reproduced Loper’s signature. In May, a stranger reached out over Instagram to warn Loper that his pen name had appeared in an image output by the chatbot. Over the summer, Loper found additional examples in a Reddit forum about ChatGPT, where users had been posting similar New Yorker-style cartoons they had generated.

Loper already knew his work was “out there, getting harvested for all of this [AI] training,” he said. But an image generator faking his signature felt more personal. “I’m not a territorial person, but my name is my name. It felt very much like a violation of my personhood.”

“The signature for me is the certificate of authenticity. I only put it on work that I’m putting on the internet that I feel needs to be recognized as from my hand,” Loper told me. “If I put my name on it, it’s official, it’s mine. It really is a brand. It’s the mark that I made.”

Loper isn’t the only New Yorker cartoonist whose signature has been reproduced by ChatGPT. In the same online forums are dozens of images with those of other prominent contributors, including Harry Bliss, Emily Flake, Joe Dator, Pat Byrnes, Peter Vey, and Jason Adam Katzenstein. In my own tests, ChatGPT output cartoons with signatures of some of the magazine’s most established cartoonists, past and present, including George Booth, Liza Donnelly, Ellis Rosen, and Saul Steinberg. In all, I documented more than 15 New Yorker cartoonists whose signatures have been used by OpenAI’s image generator without permission or compensation.

“We believe the future of creativity is one that is fundamentally human, and our focus is on building tools that empower human creativity and creators,” said a spokesperson for OpenAI in a statement. “We very much appreciate the community flagging bugs and unintended behavior by our models, so we can address them.”

After I notified OpenAI of the issue, ChatGPT began to output a new message when I asked it to generate New Yorker-style cartoons: “This prompt may violate our guardrails concerning similarity to third-party content.” Still, as of the publication of this story, it continues to sign some of the generic cartoons it generates with the names of real New Yorker cartoonists.

In my tests, ChatGPT regularly generated cartoons with the hallmarks of the 101-year-old magazine’s house style: a black-and-white, single-panel illustration with a sparse background, clean linework, and a sardonic caption — or at least, an approximation of one. Some of ChatGPT’s punch lines don’t make sense.

Not every image came with a signature, and some included pen names that were gibberish. But the signatures that did appear were regularly those of real contributors to the magazine, including older cartoonists, like Warren Miller, who published in the 1960s.

“I can see the DNA of my work in there, but it still doesn’t look like something I drew,” said Emily Flake, who’s been a New Yorker contributor since 2008. Several ChatGPT-generated cartoons posted online are signed with her pen name, “e. flake.” “It’s kind of like seeing a distant cousin.”

The character stances and shading contained echoes of Flake’s visual identity, but she said overall they looked more like amalgamations of several different cartoonists’ illustration styles. Each signature, though, was undeniably hers. “It’s like somebody attributed a quote to me that I didn’t say.”

In 2024, Condé Nast, The New Yorker’s parent company, signed a multi-year licensing deal with OpenAI allowing it to use much of the publisher’s content in its products. The terms of the deal aren’t public, but a spokesperson for The New Yorker told me Condé Nast has never granted an LLM developer permission to train models on its cartoons. Some ChatGPT creations reproduced The New Yorker’s logo alongside cartoons; that is also not allowed in any LLM deals, the spokesperson said.

Even if Condé Nast did want to license cartoons to OpenAI, The New Yorker’s standard cartoonist contract leaves little room for it. The magazine’s two cartoon editors work with a roster of freelancers who submit their work on spec and only get paid if a cartoon is selected for publication. I reviewed several templatized contracts for New Yorker contributing cartoonists, none of which permit licensing for AI training purposes. While The New Yorker has the right to publish commissioned cartoons first, it is not a “work for hire” arrangement and the cartoonist retains ownership of their copyright.

So how did OpenAI’s models learn those signatures? It’s possible they were scraped from the internet. Court documents released last month in the ongoing New York Times v. OpenAI lawsuit reveal the extent to which OpenAI knowingly circumvented publishers’ paywalls while developing ChatGPT. Unredacted Microsoft memos described ChatGPT as a “product that destroys its supply chain” and the data scraped to train its underlying LLMs as “the largest theft of labor in human history.”

In another memo, Jack Clark, then the policy director of OpenAI, wrote, “[O]ur work on AI and Creativity is going to increasingly lead to us creating systems that substitute for the labor of the people that define the ‘culture’ of society.” (Clark went on to co-found Anthropic.)

“It’s an uncanny simulacrum of an impression of a joke,” said Jason Adam Katzenstein, who has been publishing cartoons in The New Yorker since 2014. “But it’s not the point for it to actually be funny or good. The point is that it’s trying to deal a death blow to labor. It’s trying to render individual cartoonists obsolete because we cost money and take time.”

Katzenstein was part of the class action lawsuit filed against Anthropic in 2024 by members of the Authors Guild, the largest professional organization for published writers in the United States. Katzenstein’s cartoons had been used in an anthology published by Harper Collins, which was pirated and used by Anthropic to train its Claude models.

Last year, a judge ruled that training Claude on the authors’ work was fair use, but that Anthropic’s decision to download and maintain copies of the pirated books was a form of mass copyright infringement. In July, a federal court approved a settlement in the case, granting a $1.5 billion payout to authors and publishers — the largest in the history of U.S. copyright law.

Katzenstein considers the reproduction of his signature by ChatGPT to be more than just a violation of intellectual property; to him, it’s closer to false impersonation. “[ChatGPT] is attaching my name to work that I do not endorse or like. It’s slop, and unlike the other slop that I’ve encountered, this is slop that’s pretending to be me.”

Several cartoonists I spoke to also differentiated ChatGPT’s ability to mimic their illustration style from the reproduction of their signature.

“I’ve had people hack my credit card,” said Joe Dator, a New Yorker contributor for the past 20 years. “That feels like less of a violation than this. When they hacked my credit card, they didn’t dress up like me.”

U.S. intellectual property case law has yet to catch up with the rise of AI image generators, but the courts are also likely to treat these issues as distinct. Any copyright infringement claim, for example, would most likely hinge on ChatGPT’s reproduction of each cartoonist’s specific drawing style.

“[The signature] is an indication of authenticity, but attribution is a very small part of the fair use inquiry,” said James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. The chief legal challenge in a copyright suit, he said, is that ChatGPT isn’t usually reproducing any specific cartoon in these examples; rather, it’s mimicking a more general style.

Other cartoonists have filed copyright lawsuits against companies building AI image generators. One class-action led by the illustrator Sarah Anderson against Stability AI, Deviant Art, and Midjourney has been winding its way through the courts since 2023, but there is no reference to signatures in that filing.

While I found no evidence that these AI-generated cartoons are being bought or sold, there are signs that image generators are already displacing the work of professional cartoonists.

Last year, The Baltimore Sun fired Kevin Kallaugher, a Pulitzer finalist who had published editorial cartoons in the paper for more than 30 years. And earlier this year, the Sun began regularly publishing AI-generated cartoons in its opinions section. A quick check with OpenAI’s watermark identification tool shows the illustrations were created with OpenAI’s products.

“[We] condemn the use of AI for its theft from artists, its misuse of our planet’s resources, and its threat to original, creative thought,” Marc Murphy, the president of The Association of American Editorial Cartoonists, wrote in an open letter published last month. “The Sun is not alone among American newspapers taking this degrading way out.”

The New Yorker hasn’t taken any such turn toward publishing AI-generated cartoons, though none of the contributors I spoke to said they could support themselves solely on their commissions from the magazine. A New Yorker cartoon is a calling card, and work for the publication opens doors to commercial work, book illustrations, and other gigs that together make up a livelihood. It is this work that is most threatened by AI, they said.

In 1998, Pat Byrnes published his first cartoon in The New Yorker under the pen name “P.Byrnes.” He went on to build a decades-long career with that name. Since he first began drawing cartoons as a teenager, he has always signed it with a period at the end.

“It was like signing a letter,” he said. “Here’s my statement — my gift to you to accept or reject.”

Across the more than a dozen ChatGPT cartoons I found signed with Byrnes’ name, every one ended with a period.

title: Where's the Quality?
description: Just over a year ago, I resigned from my position as a staff software engineer and left the industry for about 6 months, during which I substitute taught public schools. It was a great break and much needed after building a startup from 5 to 50 engineers and taking another one through an acquisition.
fullText:
Just over a year ago, I resigned from my position as a staff software engineer and left the industry for about 6 months, during which I substitute taught public schools. It was a great break and much needed after building a startup from 5 to 50 engineers and taking another one through an acquisition.

In February I accepted a software engineering position and I’ve enjoyed it. However, the company is very much “in” on “AI”1, as it seems most every company is these days, so I’ve been making heavy use of my company provided Claude Code plan. In fact, I rarely even open my text editor anymore. Most of the code I read is in my git client and our git host. I would say I’m roughly the equivalent of a really good quality assurance engineer2. I spend most of my time reviewing Claude’s code, reviewing team member’s pull requests that were also written in Claude Code, and manually testing mine and my team member’s work. I think I probably get more “done” than I did before the AIpocalypse, which is probably a good thing.

However, I still have one lingering question. If the AI tools are truly miraculous, why isn’t the quality of software getting better? Is it getting better and I’m just not noticing it? For example, is there a product or service that is fundamentally more functional than it was 5 years ago? Is there a company that is able to leverage AI to create higher quality products? It’s clear that we’re shipping more software than perhaps we ever have, but it also feels like the overall quality of the shipped code is probably lower than the average quality was before AI.

You would perhaps think that the companies developing and shipping the AI tools would be some of the best examples of what AI coding can really do, but even they seem to not be able to maintain uptimes or ship updates that are free of breaking bugs. Call me jaded, but I think the current version of Windows might be the worst Microsoft has ever shipped. If I’m being completely honest, macOS, iOS, etc. are not far behind. I recently acquired an iPhone 4 running iOS 6 and I was taken aback at how well it runs. Where is the “year of the Linux Desktop” distro at? What are we spending all these tokens on, really? I’m genuinely asking. If you have an example of software that you feel is fundamentally better than what we’ve had before, please email me or leave a reply to let me know.

For me, the best part of the AI tools is the fun random stuff. Claude is really good at ssh’ing into some linux box and doing some boutique one-off task. For example, one of my hobbies is buying random old routers from the thrift store, cracking them open, hooking up to the UART serial port, and poking around. Claude was really good at getting into u-boot and even compiling some custom code to make the LEDs blink. It was fun! But it was also basically useless beyond the fun.

In response to a reader asking me about “vibe coding”, I pointed out that commodification of code is not new. Offshoring to the cheapest contractor available has been a thing for at least 30 years, and the age-old adage “you get what you pay for” very much applies. AI tokens are probably still cheaper than the cheapest contractor on Fiverr ever was, and honestly the quality is probably better than the cheap contractor. But that’s a pretty low bar to shoot for.

Instead, I think we should shoot for software excellence. I believe in all aspects of life we should strive to be virtuous. Admittedly I am an Eagle Scout so maybe I was just indoctrinated into a false worldview, but I strongly believe that anything good or worthwhile in this world is the result of someone caring, working hard, and doing what is morally right.

As software engineers, we must be filled with empathy for the end users, even when the business is not. We must find ways to deliver quality as well as the speed and feature set demanded by the market. In my opinion, this has always been the literal definition of “engineering”. Technicians simply follow instructions. Artists imagine a world where there are no constraints. Engineering is somewhere in the middle. We take real world constraints, demands of the customer and business, and use our ingenuity and creativity to deliver something incredible that we are proud of even when nobody else cares or notices. Something “insanely great” as the great poet used to say.

I’ve talked before about the “curse” of being a software developer. Perhaps this all is just born out of some existential guilt, knowing I’m responsible for potentially ruining someone’s day because of a bug I shipped. As much as possible, I want to write software that delights and improves lives. I don’t want to build bad systems that become a kind of prison for the end user, a system they are forced to live in.

In the age of AI, where code has never been cheaper and easier to produce, we should refocus our industry on quality. We should put an end to “move fast and break things” because we can. We can move fast, and ship high quality products that enhance our community. We should strive for excellence in our work.

I don’t actually believe we’re anywhere close to “artificial intelligence”, but I’ll call LLM tools “AI” just because that’s the common vernacular these days. ↩

I never really understood why we call QA folks “engineers” since in my experience most of them just do manual testing. ↩

title: Example.com Just Launched the Biggest Redesign in Decades
description: A look at the history of visual changes to example.com.
fullText:
example.com is a reserved domain name set aside by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) for documentation purposes. It has been available as an example URL for developers and writers since the late nineties. While the overall messaging of the page has been consistent over time, the visual appearance has received several major overhauls. In this article, we take a look at the recent changes as well as the evolution of example.com over the last 20+ years. Until 28 September 2026, example.com was a static English-language page. The redesign introduces multi-language support using JavaScript, showing the content in a new language every 5 seconds. Example.com shows an explanation of the site's purpose in English, Arabic, Chinese, French, Russian and Spanish. This is the English-language message: This domain is for use in documentation examples without needing permission. This is not a service, avoid relying on it for testing and monitoring purposes. Along with introducing multi-language support, the JavaScript code also inserts an SVG book icon. The new site doesn't just replace the content when showing the next language. Instead, there's a gradual opacity transition. The opacity animation itself just uses transition: opacity .4s;. But how is the character-by-character transition implemented? Each character is wrapped in its own span element, and each span gets a slightly larger CSS transition-delay than the one before it. That means each character's opacity animation happens at a slightly different time. IANA provided the following statement explaining the reasoning behind the recent changes: The changes we make to the site from time-to-time are usually informed by a desire to either reduce the overall bandwidth demands of serving the site, or improve its utility. At its heart it is a placeholder for a site no-one should be accessing, but we have historically showed a message there to inform visitors about why the domain is registered and how they may use it. As it tends to be heavily trafficked, the overall bandwidth is a key consideration, and to that end one of the changes we made this week was to split the page content into a more basic page, augmented by a separate Javascript file with additional content beyond that. Since most of the traffic to the site is automated it tends not to fetch the Javascript file, reducing overall data requirements. The fundamental purpose of the domain is for use in documentation, such as illustrative examples you may find in instructions. We know that people may, for example, cut-and-paste a sample configuration file and forget to customize entries that contain an example domain, and we expect we get some incidental traffic from that. However, the domain isn't intended to be a general purpose endpoint for things like availability testing so we do not encourage that kind of usage. There is no requirement there is a HTTP service present on the host in order to fulfill its purpose, we just operate it as a courtesy. According to Wikipedia, the example.com website launched on January 1, 1999. The earliest version available to view in the Wayback Machine is from January 20, 2002. The earliest version of the website only featured a list of domain names reserved by the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) and IANA. In the .com, .net, and .org top-level domains (TLDs), various domain names are reserved. These names are reserved from initial registration, but to the extent they are already registered the existing registrant may renew them. Structurally, the HTML used a table layout, with the ICANN logo positioned in the top left corner of the page. The server headers show that the site used Apache 1.3.22 at this point. The first version of the example.com wording we recognize today came 67 days after the first available screenshot: You have reached this web page by typing "example.com", "example.net", or "example.org" into your web browser. These domain names are reserved for use in documentation and are not available for registration. In February 2003, the content was amended to include a link to RFC 2606, the official document for reserved top-level and second-level domains, so visitors could find more information on the website's purpose. There was also a small technical change around this time: the server was upgraded to Apache 1.3.27 on Red Hat Linux. The website then went unchanged for seven years. On July 30, 2010, a slight change was made: example.edu was now pointed to the landing page, alongside the three previous domains. From January 2011, example.com didn't serve its own page. Instead, it redirected visitors to a page on IANA's website. That changed on July 29, 2013, when the redirect was removed and example.com began serving its own page from the EdgeCast Content Delivery Network (CDN) instead of Apache, alongside a major redesign of the landing page. The new design used a rounded card with an

reading 'Example Domain' and a new description of the website's purpose. The viewable domain list was now gone, with a link to IANA's website A new update came six years after the biggest change in the website's history. The layout remained the same, but the font stack was modernized to include more fallback fonts for devices such as Macs, iPhones, and Windows PCs. The copy was tweaked slightly, with 'is for use in illustrative examples' replacing 'established to be used' and 'in literature' replacing 'in examples'. Almost twelve years after the switch from Apache to the EdgeCast CDN, another infrastructure change took place: the Server header disappeared entirely. The response headers alone don't reveal which platform was serving the page at this point. A change of provider around this time isn't surprising. EdgeCast had been acquired from Yahoo by Limelight Networks in 2022 and rebranded as Edgio. Edgio then filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in late 2024, with Akamai acquiring select Edgio customer contracts. Later in 2025, the page was redesigned. The card design was dropped, and the HTML was minified. The copy was changed to a more direct message, again linking to IANA's website, with the link text changed from 'More information...' to 'Learn more'. Less than a year after the previous switch, the infrastructure changed again: the site now serves from Cloudflare, as indicated by the cloudflare server header and CF-RAY header in the response. Whatever platform served the page after the January 2025 change, it has now been replaced with a Cloudflare-fronted setup. The next update, on June 9, 2026, brought no visual changes. The only HTML changes on the page itself were a favicon tag being added and the

tags being closed. The page now includes an empty favicon:

title: Worth Building
description: What changes when a tool doesn't have to pay for itself. Years ago, if an app annoyed me, I shrugged and dealt with it.
fullText:
Years ago, if an app annoyed me, I shrugged and dealt with it. I could sometimes have fixed it or built my own, but the annoyance rarely justified the effort. With LLMs that calculation has changed, and this past weekend it changed for a domain lookup tool.

Occasionally I need to check DNS records or registration info for a domain. At my computer I use dig or whois. Otherwise I Google "domain lookup tool," click on one, and paste in the domain. Most of what comes up is slow, buried in upsells, and unpleasant to use for something that should be simple.

They aren't badly made -- they're well made for a different job. A domain lookup answers a question nobody pays to ask, so many of the free tools that show up in search are the ones a sales funnel justifies: the lookup brings in someone who might buy a domain or hosting, and the page is built to rank for "domain lookup tool" and to sell. The tools you find are the ones built to be found. Being good at the lookup was never what paid for them.

I wanted something I'd actually enjoy using, so I opened Claude Code and built heade.rs. In three prompts and about an hour I had a first working version deployed to Cloudflare: DNS and registration records, live latency, email configuration, HTTPS details. The rest of the day went into making it feel good: animations, graphics, an interface I like looking at. It costs less than a cup of coffee a month to run. It doesn't have to sell anything, so it can just be good.

Before, a project like this needed justifying. I'd have asked whether I'd use it enough to make the time worthwhile. If I expected to spend weeks on it, I'd have started thinking about other users, pricing, how it could pay for itself. A small annoyance would have become a much bigger commitment; a weekend is much easier to justify. I wanted it to exist, and that was enough.

A few hours used to get a programmer a script; now it gets a polished app, and it gets a non-programmer something instead of nothing. More people can clear the bar, and more ideas clear it: small tools that solve a personal annoyance, weird ideas you're curious about, things you build simply because you'd enjoy having them or the world would be more beautiful if they existed. The audience can be one person.

The same economics cut the other way: heade.rs will probably not rank for "domain lookup tool," and neither will most things built like it. Cheaper software means more people shipping, and another demo in a crowded feed is easy to scroll past. If you want to reach more people, you still have to give them a reason to care. I'm more interested when someone explains what bothered them, what they made, and the choices they cared about along the way. The story gives me a reason to try the thing.

Sometimes sharing a personal project leads somewhere unexpected. Four years ago Paragraph started as something I built for myself, then other people wanted to use it too. I'm glad I shared it.

But I also like that heade.rs doesn't need to follow that path. If it stays a little tool I use occasionally to look up a domain, it was still worth building.

title: Por qué uso (y recomiendo) dominios .xyz numéricos para self-hosting
description: El problema  Self-hostear algo como Grafana, tu app, una API, necesita tres cosas: un nombre estable que resuelva a tu IP, un certifica...
fullText:
Self-hostear algo como Grafana, tu app, una API, necesita tres cosas: un nombre estable que resuelva a tu IP, un certificado TLS válido (Let's Encrypt no emite para IPs), y no depender de un subdominio de DDNS gratuito que puede cambiar o desaparecer. Un dominio propio resuelve las tres. El asunto es el costo y la disponibilidad del nombre.

Ahí entra la clase numérica de .xyz.

Y si hosteás desde tu casa, se suma un cuarto: el ISP normalmente no te da IP pública sino que te deja detrás de CGNAT (una IP compartida entre varios clientes). Con CGNAT el port forwarding ni siquiera funciona ya que no hay a dónde forwardear.

Un dominio propio + un túnel saliente resuelven las cuatro.

En 2017 el registro de .xyz abrió un bloque: todos los dominios de 6 a 9 dígitos con terminación .xyz (de 000000.xyz a 999999999.xyz), 1.111 mil millones de combinaciones, a US$0,99
 por año para siempre — registro, renovación y transferencia, con las tasas ICANN incluidas. La renovación cuesta lo mismo que el alta.

El dominio numérico (ej. 12345678.xyz) como raíz, con DNS en Cloudflare (gratis) y un wildcard *. Y lo clave para hostear desde casa es el Cloudflare Tunnel (el demonio cloudflared) que me dá un túnel saliente hacia Cloudflare, sin IP pública y sin abrir puertos en el router. Cada servicio tiene su subdominio (app., api., grafana.).

title: Becoming a Photographer
description: Last week the topic on everyone's mind seemed to be the future of programming. All my friends were talking about it, people I follow were talking about it,...
fullText:
Last week the topic on everyone's mind seemed to be the future of programming.
All my friends were talking about it, people I follow were talking about it, and I was
thinking about it as well. Then David's (DHH's) Rails World keynote
turbocharged the conversation.

His talk didn't come as a surprise to me. I was a week into rewriting HEY in Rust
during Rails World. And "Pencils down" only codified how we'd been working for months at
that point.

David is right. Like it or not, we programmers, like painters before us, are slowly
going to disappear. AI, like the camera, completely changed the game. You can sulk about
it, or you can pick up a camera, start learning, and become a photographer.

I was skeptical of AI and vibe coding. My initial dabbling with it didn't
turn out that well. The agents needed a lot of hand-holding
to produce a decent result. But the models improved at an incredible pace, and I got better at employing
them, learned their limitations, and learned how to express what I wanted.

For me, the first real test for this new way of working was HEY CLI.

Rob and I built it - the CLI, TUI, and the
supporting API, SDK, and
ActionCable client - over the span of a week while
he was traveling, and while I was shipping and polishing a major pricing change for Basecamp. It's
completely vibe-coded. No human has seen any of the machinations in the code beyond the initial
project setup - and it worked out!

Something clicked for me on that project. I suddenly realized that my only limit now was my
imagination.

Jason joined us late in the week to turn our programmer art
into something delightful. He did wonders in just a day - in a completely foreign medium (ASCII art),
in a programming language he doesn't know, in a codebase no human has ever read.

That got me thinking: "Maybe I could design the calendar?"

I had a vision for what the finished calendar TUI could look like, so I gave it a go.

Designing the calendar was challenging. There were dead ends and abandoned ideas, but I got it done,
I'm very happy with it, and I leveled up as a designer.

My programming skills helped me along the way. I caught things that wouldn't work and
guided the agents towards better solutions. I didn't need to write the code myself, but knowing
how software works still made me better at getting the result I wanted. And the same was true for
design. The more I learned about typography, layout, and terminal interfaces, the more
things I could imagine trying.

AI removed the speed limit, but it didn't remove the limits of my imagination. The more you
know, the more you can imagine.

Walls between previously strictly defined roles have broken down: programmer, ops, designer, QA,
mobile, web. This doesn't mean expertise is useless. Quite the opposite. A lot of what I learned
over the years carries over and helps me see possibilities, problems, and tradeoffs
I otherwise wouldn't. Merlin Rebovic gave a great talk about that.

But knowing a bit of everything gets you much further today than being excellent at one or two things.
Every new skill gives you another way of thinking, another set of things you know to look for,
and, most importantly, more things you can imagine. The future needs a more even blend of skills.

What if I told you that the photo above is the third shot out of five? Would that take away from the photo?
Is it somehow tarnished by not being perfect on the first try? By the two photos before and after it?

Of course it isn't. Nobody looks at a photograph and asks: "Yes, but how many bad exposures did you take?"

Misfires, variations, and riffing are part of the process. It takes taste to pick out the best one and
to polish it up.

It's the same when working with agents.

We used to turn an idea into code, then meticulously polish that code to excellence, and ship it.
Every idea had to prove its place; every line of code had to be worth the time it took to write and
think about it. Writing code used to be expensive, but it isn't anymore!

Now I can turn an idea into something real in minutes, play around with it, get a feel for it, and then
iterate on it or throw it away. The first attempt will probably be rubbish. That's okay. Every attempt
and iteration teaches me something about where I want to go next.

There will be false starts, rabbit holes, and bugs. There will be things that fall through the cracks.
Excellence doesn't have to happen on the first try. It can be eventual.

I can try five ideas in the time it previously took me to prove just one. Four might not work out. But,
just like the four photos you never saw, that doesn't diminish the one that worked.

The goal is still excellence. We just don't need it at every step of the way anymore.

If I'm no longer writing the code, what exactly am I doing? If you ponder that question, let me
ask you another one: Do civil engineers do engineering?

My mom is a civil engineer. I have tons of memories of her at her giant drawing table with rice paper,
rulers, pens, and razor blades, designing people's homes. With her pen she dug trenches, laid rebar,
set walls, and picked the type of concrete to use without ever picking up a shovel. She was doing
engineering. She was solving hard problems with hard constraints. The fact that someone else picked
up a shovel, cut the rebar, set up molds, and poured the concrete doesn't take that away from her.

So don't conflate writing code with engineering.

With the agents pouring concrete, we can now focus on the thing as a whole. Not just how to
implement it, but how to design it, test it, deploy it, make it accessible, bring it to other
platforms, announce it, promote it, and charge for it. Instead of designing walls, we'll design
homes.

Programmers will disappear, but engineering software won't. It will morph into something broader,
something that's a little bit of everything. We have to become makers.

Picking up a camera won't instantly make you a photographer. Most of us walk around with a
great camera in our pockets, yet few of us are actually good at using it.

If you take a single picture, compare it to the subject, and
conclude "this is rubbish," that doesn't necessarily mean the camera is bad.
You have to learn how to use it. Learn its limitations and how to work around them.

Like painters in the 19th century, we are in uncharted territory. Nobody really knows what
they're doing or what being good at photography even means. We're all exploring this new
space and trying to figure things out, some with more success than others.

There's only one way to find out where this goes: pick up the camera.

title: You're Leaving Compute on the Table
description: Six computers on one desk, a 2001 supercomputer's worth of compute, spending most of the day displaying spinners.
fullText:
There are six computers on my table right now.

All of them are awake. None of them are working. The hardest job any of them will do in the next hour is draw a spinner: waiting on a machine in Virginia to finish work whose every input is already sitting on this desk.

This desk is not unusual. Whoever your customers are, something like it is sitting in front of them. And for the most part, what’s on mine is more than capable of serving me.

Let’s look at what we have here:

All of this sits on my table and draws roughly 100 watts under load, about as much as an incandescent lightbulb.

For perspective: the Apollo Guidance Computer ran at roughly 85,000 instructions per second, with 4 KB of RAM, and weighed almost 32 kilograms. Deep Blue reached about 11 GFLOPS. The ~15 TFLOPS on this table would have been the fastest supercomputer on Earth in 2001. Compute that once required a room, a government, or a world-champion chess match now sits in the general-purpose devices I use to watch cat videos.

Almost nothing I do each day touches the ceiling of this hardware.

Yet every time I open X, I see another product launching online that could, or should, run locally. I’ve shipped these too.

It takes data and context already on my computer, sends them to a machine in Virginia, performs the work there, and sends the result back. The builder pays to create another execution environment; the customer already has one.

That duplication is the waste. Not every HTTP request. Not every server. Work whose data and context already live on the user’s machine, the machine sitting right in front of the person who wants the result.

Sun Microsystems spent two decades telling the industry that “the network is the computer.” The industry finally believed it, right as it stopped being true. The network is the phone book. The computer is the computer.

The internet gives people a permanent, addressable presence. It lets parties discover one another, communicate, and establish shared state.

Servers exist so parties can find each other and agree on what’s true. Everything else is waste.

Servers are excellent at coordination, authority, persistence, and work too large for the client. But computation should have to earn its trip across the network.

Software that runs locally is cheaper to build on and easier to trust. And it keeps working when the internet doesn’t.

“Zero marginal cost” is true for compute, not for engineering. Client-side software means a larger testing matrix, hostile machines, weak devices, and need for a robust update pipeline. The capacity is already paid for; making it dependable is not.

But that price was set a decade ago, when dependable meant a QA lab full of laptops and a hand-rolled updater. Wasm gave us one runtime everywhere; update pipelines are commodity; the testing matrix is exactly the kind of grunt work models now do. Most builders are working from a quote they never re-requested.

Some work belongs on a server. People want data synced across devices. Providers cannot trust clients to report billing honestly. Old and weak devices still exist. Long-running tasks should survive a closed laptop. Google Docs beat desktop Office on zero install, no data loss, and access from any device. And frontier models are unlikely to fit on your machine anytime soon.

Those are not edge cases. They are the boundary of the argument. The only question is which side of that boundary your product actually sits on. Checked, not assumed.

But games never had the luxury of ignoring the client. Physics forced the architecture: a data center can stream frames, but latency is a law of physics, and you don’t get to repeal physics. So game developers put latency-sensitive physics, rendering, and interaction on the player’s machine, while servers arbitrate the shared world: who is where, who hit whom, and what counts as true.

The client computes. The server coordinates.

Nothing about that split is specific to games. Figma’s renderer was written in C++, compiled to WebAssembly, and runs in the browser. The server handles the shared document and collaboration. It does not draw every rectangle in us-east-1 and mail the pixels back.

And now there is Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. The model may live on a server, but the harness lives where the code, tools, credentials, and developer already are. The server streams intelligence; the client gives it hands.

That is the form factor people like because it does not pretend the computer in front of them is a dumb terminal.

AI has made the old mistake expensive enough to notice again. Builders now pay per second for cloud sandboxes that poorly imitate a laptop: cloning repositories, rebuilding environments, copying secrets, and reconstructing context that already exists on the user’s machine.

Sometimes that is the right trade. Background agents need persistence. Untrusted code needs isolation. Large jobs need hardware the customer does not own. But “put the harness in the cloud” should be a conclusion, not a default.

So the answer to “what should we do about it” is a default, not a product. When you design the next feature, sort the work into two piles: state that other parties must agree on, and everything else. The first pile earns a server. The second pile already has a computer: the one your customer is looking at.

Notice what the first pile keeps: identity, billing, the source of truth. Everything you actually charge for. Moving the compute doesn’t move the meter.

Take the last feature you shipped. Which pile did most of the work sit in, and which pile did you build it in?

Consumer hardware has become absurdly capable. The industry has treated that capability as somebody else’s problem.

The photo at the top of this essay hasn’t changed. Six computers, maybe 100 watts. Tomorrow they will spend most of the day displaying spinners, waiting on Virginia for work they could do themselves.

title: 4 ways the midterm elections could turn out, with a month to go
description:
Democrats are heading into the last month of the midterm elections campaign with ambitions going deeper and deeper into red territory, while Republicans are grim about their hopes of holding on to either chamber of Congress.
